lessons.title: Block devices: disks, sectors and loop devices
lessons.goal:
Learn what a block device is, how to list the disks of a machine, and how to practise safely with a **loop device**: an ordinary file presented to the kernel as a disk.

Why it matters: you will partition, format, grow and repair disks. Practising on files costs nothing and cannot damage real data.

setup.note: These steps use sudo, loop devices (files that act as disks) and partitioning tools. They never touch your real disks. Every loop device is detached at the end.

steps.title: Block versus character devices
steps.text: A **block device** gives random access to fixed-size blocks (disks, SSDs, partitions). A **character device** is a stream (terminal, `/dev/null`). In `ls -l` the first letter is `b` or `c`. The two numbers are the **major** (driver) and **minor** (instance).

steps.title: List the disks
steps.text: `lsblk` shows the tree: disk, partitions, and what is built on them (LVM, mounts). `-d` shows only whole disks.

run.output:
NAME SIZE TYPE ROTA
sda   50G disk    1

steps.title: Sector sizes
steps.text: A disk is addressed in **sectors**, traditionally 512 bytes (many modern disks are 4096). `blockdev` reads the geometry.

steps.title: Make a practice disk
steps.text: `truncate -s 64M disk.img` creates a **sparse** file: it claims 64 MB but uses no disk space until written. `losetup` attaches it to a free loop device. The kernel then treats `/dev/loopN` like a disk.

run.cmd: truncate -s 64M disk.img; ls -ls disk.img | awk '{print "allocated KB:", $1, "apparent bytes:", $6}'

steps.title: The kernel sees a disk
steps.text: Reading the device gives zeros (the file is empty). The size matches the file. Detach when done.

run.cmd: sudo dd if=$L bs=512 count=1 status=none | xxd | head -n 1

steps.under: Block I/O goes through the **block layer**: the file system submits `bio` requests, the I/O scheduler (module 22) orders them, and the driver talks to the hardware. A loop device is a driver whose "hardware" is reads and writes on a file.

quiz.q: Which letter marks a block device in `ls -l`?

options: A file presented to the kernel as a block device
quiz.explain: It lets you practise on files.

options: A full 64 MB file on disk
A sparse file that uses space only when written

quiz.q: What are major and minor numbers?
quiz.explain: They identify the driver and the unit.

check.scenario: You must rehearse resizing a production LVM volume. How do you build a safe test bed without spare disks?
check.answer: Create sparse files (`truncate -s 1G a.img b.img`), attach them with `losetup`, and build the same PV/VG/LV structure on the loop devices. Everything can be thrown away by detaching the devices and deleting the files.

lessons.title: Partition tables: GPT versus MBR
lessons.goal:
Learn what a partition table is, create one with `parted`, and compare the two formats by looking at the bytes on disk.

Why it matters: MBR limits you to 2 TiB and four primary partitions; GPT is the standard for UEFI. When a disk "shows no partitions" or a boot fails, you read these structures.

setup.note: These steps use sudo, loop devices (files that act as disks) and partitioning tools. They never touch your real disks. Every loop device is detached at the end.

steps.title: A partition table is a few bytes at the start
steps.text: The partition table says where each partition starts and ends. It lives in the first sectors of the disk. We create a 64 MB image and write a **GPT** table with two partitions.

run.cmd: truncate -s 64M gpt.img; L=$(sudo losetup -f --show -P gpt.img); echo $L
sudo parted -s $L mklabel gpt mkpart data 1MiB 32MiB mkpart logs 32MiB 100%
sudo parted -s $L unit s print | sed -n '1,12p' | grep -vE '^(Model|Sector|Disk Flags)?$'
run.output:
Model: Loopback device (loopback)
Disk /dev/loop0: 131072s
Sector size (logical/physical): 512B/512B
Partition Table: gpt
Disk Flags: 
Number  Start   End      Size    File system  Name  Flags
 1      2048s   65535s   63488s               data
 2      65536s  131038s  65503s               logs

steps.title: The partitions become devices
steps.text: With `-P` (scan partitions) the kernel creates `loop0p1` and `loop0p2`.

run.output:
NAME      SIZE TYPE PARTLABEL
loop0      64M loop 
├─loop0p1  31M part data
└─loop0p2  32M part logs

steps.title: GPT on disk: signature and backup
steps.text: GPT keeps a **protective MBR** in sector 0 (so old tools see a full disk), the GPT header at sector 1 starting with the text `EFI PART`, and a **backup header** in the last sector. The backup lets tools repair a damaged table.
steps.after: `55aa` at offset 510 is the boot signature of the protective MBR. `EFI PART` is the GPT header, found twice: at the start and at the very end.

steps.title: MBR on disk: four entries of 16 bytes
steps.text: An **MBR** (also called msdos) table is 64 bytes at offset 446: four entries of 16 bytes each, then the signature `55aa`. Each entry stores a type, a start sector and a size as 32-bit numbers, which is where the 2 TiB limit comes from.

run.cmd: sudo losetup -d $L; truncate -s 64M mbr.img; L=$(sudo losetup -f --show -P mbr.img)
sudo parted -s $L mklabel msdos mkpart primary 1MiB 32MiB

steps.title: Compare
steps.text:
- **MBR**: 4 primary partitions (or 3 + extended), disks up to 2 TiB, no backup copy, no checksums, boots with BIOS.
- **GPT**: 128 partitions by default, disks up to 8 ZiB, backup header, CRC32 checksums, partition names and UUIDs, needed for UEFI boot and disks above 2 TiB.
steps.under: Both formats store sector numbers. GPT uses 64-bit logical block addresses (LBA), so it addresses 2^64 sectors; MBR uses 32-bit LBA values, so 2^32 sectors x 512 bytes = 2 TiB.

quiz.q: What text starts the GPT header?
Why can MBR not address more than 2 TiB?
Where is the backup GPT header?
options: In the last sector of the disk

check.scenario: A 6 TB disk shows only 2 TB usable after you partitioned it with fdisk on an old server. What went wrong?
check.answer: The disk got an **MBR** (msdos) label, which cannot address beyond 2 TiB. Convert to GPT (`parted /dev/sdX mklabel gpt`, which **destroys** the old table: back up first, or use `sgdisk -g` for a non-destructive conversion), then recreate the partitions.

lessons.title: Alignment, saving partition tables and UUIDs
lessons.goal:
Learn why partitions start at 1 MiB, how to dump and restore a partition table, and how partitions and file systems get stable identifiers.

Why it matters: misaligned partitions slow down SSDs and RAID; scripted layouts make servers reproducible; and device names like `/dev/sdb` can change between boots while UUIDs do not.

setup.note: These steps use sudo, loop devices (files that act as disks) and partitioning tools. They never touch your real disks. Every loop device is detached at the end.

steps.title: Alignment
steps.text: Modern disks use 4 KiB physical sectors and SSDs write in larger pages. A partition that starts on a boundary the hardware likes is **aligned**. The standard is to start at sector 2048 (1 MiB). `parted align-check` tests it.

run.cmd: truncate -s 128M a.img; L=$(sudo losetup -f --show -P a.img); sudo parted -s $L mklabel gpt mkpart p1 1MiB 64MiB mkpart p2 64MiB 100%
sudo parted -s $L align-check optimal 1 && echo 'partition 1: aligned'; sudo parted -s $L align-check optimal 2 && echo 'partition 2: aligned'

steps.after: Partition 1 starts at sector 2048 (1 MiB). The size is in 512-byte sectors: 63 MiB = 129024 sectors.

steps.title: Dump and restore a layout
steps.text: `sfdisk -d` prints the partition table as text. Feed it to `sfdisk` on another disk to clone the layout. This is how you script server builds and how you save a table before changing it.

run.cmd: sudo sfdisk -d $L > layout.txt; grep -vE '^(device|sector-size|first-lba|last-lba)' layout.txt | sed 's#/dev/loop[0-9]*#DISK#'
run.output:
label: gpt
label-id: 58681C4D-F11A-480E-988D-4ABCD95C374E
unit: sectors

DISKp1 : start=        2048, size=      129024, type=0FC63DAF-8483-4772-8E79-3D69D8477DE4, uuid=3230C3D9-E55C-4F5B-AAFD-5D28B73F8E54, name="p1"
DISKp2 : start=      131072, size=      131039, type=0FC63DAF-8483-4772-8E79-3D69D8477DE4, uuid=AF54A409-A4DD-409E-92A9-6C65643F1718, name="p2"

run.cmd: truncate -s 128M b.img; M=$(sudo losetup -f --show -P b.img); sudo sfdisk -q $M < layout.txt; sleep 1; lsblk -no NAME,SIZE $M | sed 's/^/clone: /'

steps.title: Stable names: UUIDs
steps.text: A **PARTUUID** identifies a partition (stored in the GPT). A **UUID** identifies a file system (stored in its superblock). `/dev/sdb2` may become `/dev/sdc2` after a reboot; UUIDs never change. Use them in `/etc/fstab` and boot arguments.

run.cmd: sudo mkfs.ext4 -q ${L}p1; sudo blkid -s TYPE -s UUID -s PARTLABEL ${L}p1 | sed -E 's/UUID="[^"]*"/UUID="<uuid>"/; s#/dev/loop[0-9]+#/dev/loopN#'

steps.under: `udev` creates the symlinks in `/dev/disk/by-uuid`, `by-partuuid`, `by-label` and `by-id` when a device appears, by reading the identifiers with `blkid`. They point to whatever kernel name the device got this time.

steps.title: Clean up
steps.text: Detach the loop devices and delete the images.

run.cmd: sudo losetup -d $L $M; rm -f a.img b.img gpt.img mbr.img disk.img; losetup -a | wc -l

quiz.q: At which sector does a standard aligned first partition start?
Which tool dumps a partition table as a script?

options: Device names like /dev/sdb can change between boots

quiz.q: What stores a file system's UUID?

check.scenario: After adding a disk, the server boots to emergency mode because `/data` (listed as /dev/sdb1 in fstab) is missing or mounted wrong. What is the lasting fix?
check.answer: Use stable identifiers in `/etc/fstab`: `UUID=... /data xfs defaults,nofail 0 2` (get it with `blkid`), and `nofail` so a missing data disk does not stop the boot. Verify with `findmnt --verify` before rebooting.

interview.a: A device with random access to fixed-size blocks, like a disk or partition, exposed as a file in /dev. See [the lesson](#/lesson/19/block-devices).

interview.q: How can you practise partitioning without a spare disk?
interview.a: Create a sparse file with `truncate`, attach it with `losetup -P`, and use it like a disk.

GPT: 64-bit LBA, up to 128 partitions, backup header, checksums, needed for UEFI and disks over 2 TiB. MBR: 32-bit LBA (2 TiB limit), 4 primary partitions, no backup. See [the lesson](#/lesson/19/gpt-vs-mbr).
To align with 4 KiB physical sectors, SSD pages and RAID stripes, avoiding read-modify-write slowdowns.

interview.q: Why use UUIDs instead of /dev/sdX in fstab?
interview.a: Kernel device names depend on probe order and can change. UUIDs are stored in the file system. See [the lesson](#/lesson/19/alignment-sfdisk-uuid).

interview.q: How do you copy a partition layout to another disk?
interview.a: `sfdisk -d /dev/sda | sfdisk /dev/sdb`, or `sgdisk -R` for GPT (then randomise the GUIDs with `sgdisk -G`).

glossary.def: A device with random access to fixed-size blocks, such as a disk.
A block device backed by a regular file.
The smallest addressable unit of a disk (512 or 4096 bytes).
GUID Partition Table: modern partition table with backup header and checksums.
Master Boot Record: the legacy partition table with 4 entries and 32-bit sector numbers.
Starting partitions on boundaries that match the hardware's physical blocks.
A stable identifier stored in a file system or partition.
